# Fairness statement - Task 12 (counterfactual audit of the Task 11 resume screener)

*Generated by `scripts/run_task12.py` from the numbers in this folder; nothing here is typed in by hand.*

## What was tested
The Task 11 screener (60% TF-IDF similarity + 40% required-skill overlap, score in [0, 1]) was audited with **25 counterfactual twin pairs**
(`resume_bias_pairs`). In each pair the two resumes have identical skills and experience and differ only in a gender-coded candidate name
(and, for 13 pairs, the college tier);
12 pairs change the name only. A fair screener must give both the same score
(`expected_score_difference = 0`). Twins isolate the effect of the protected attribute: any score difference cannot be explained by qualifications.
Protected attributes available for this audit: inferred_gender, college_tier. Protected values were used only for aggregate auditing and never as scoring inputs. Tolerance: a twin gap above 0.01 (one point on a 0-100 view) counts as material.

## Results (primary job per pair; 25 pairs)
| Screener | Average gap | Median | Maximum | Non-zero pairs | Above tolerance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Task 11 as shipped (before) | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0 | 0 |
| Task 11 given resume text only (before) | 0.000180 | 0.000152 | 0.000677 | 25 | 0 |
| Task 12 fair screener (after) | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0 | 0 |

* **Average twin gap before / after:** shipped Task 11 0.000000 -> 0.000000; text-only Task 11 0.000180 -> 0.000000.
* **Percentage reduction:** 100.0% versus the text-only baseline; **not defined versus the shipped Task 11 (its gap was already 0, so there was nothing to reduce)**.
* Both gaps were far below the tolerance: the largest baseline gap was 0.000677 against 0.01. Task 11 was **not** materially biased on these twins; its protection came from scrubbing the *values of structured columns*,
  and the audit shows that protection disappears when only text is supplied (small but non-zero gaps in 25/25 pairs). In the text-only run, male-coded names scored higher in 13 pairs, lower in 12 and tied in 0 (mean male - female = +0.000054; sign test p = 1.000). The size is about 1/100 of the tolerance, so it is a measurable sensitivity, not a material gap.
* Robustness: over all 10 jobs (250 pair-job comparisons) the text-only average gap is 0.000035 and the fair screener's is 0.000000.

## Where the differences came from (measured)
| variant | mean_gap_primary_job | max_gap_primary_job | nonzero_pairs_primary_job |
|---|---|---|---|
| nothing masked (raw text) | 0.000463 | 0.002732 | 25 |
| e-mail/URL only | 0.000179 | 0.000663 | 25 |
| institution tier only | 0.000467 | 0.002783 | 25 |
| name only | 0.000142 | 0.000387 | 21 |
| name + e-mail | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0 |
| name + e-mail + location | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0 |
| all categories (task12_fair) | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0 |

The twins differ **only** in header name, contact line (name-bearing e-mail) and, for some pairs, the institution-tier statement; there are 0 other differing lines.
Skill and experience extraction was identical for twins in every pair-job comparison. All residual score differences are TF-IDF effects (rare name tokens change the vector norm); skill-overlap gaps were 0.
Masking the name alone or the e-mail alone is **not** enough; both are needed. Institution tier did not leak in this pipeline only because Task 11 drops numeric tokens ("Tier 1" and "Tier 2" are textually identical after preprocessing) - an accidental, fragile protection that the fair screener now makes explicit.

## What changed
`fair_preprocessing.py` masks personal information from the resume text itself (name, e-mail, location prefix, phone, institution-tier statement, age / date of birth, personal-detail fields, gendered titles, pronouns, graduation years), and the fair screener is given only `resume_id` and `resume_text` (feature isolation).
Skills, certifications, degree subjects, job titles, employers and the experience statement are **not** masked. The Task 11 engine is reused unchanged; the original screener stays available (`task11_as_shipped`, `task11_text_only`).
Not hard-coded to any pair. A **synthetic stress test** (not part of the 25 pairs: 31 real resumes, one at a time, with only the sensitive tokens varied or a personal-details block added) checks the pathways the twins cannot reach (mean / max gap):

| perturbation | task11_text_only_mean_gap | task12_fair_mean_gap | task11_text_only_max_gap | task12_fair_max_gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| age_and_date_of_birth_disclosed | 0.008232 | 0.000000 | 0.014554 | 0.000000 |
| gender_and_marital_status_disclosed | 0.004729 | 0.000000 | 0.008326 | 0.000000 |
| gendered_title_Mr_vs_Ms | 0.000976 | 0.000000 | 0.002390 | 0.000000 |
| graduation_year_old_vs_recent | 0.001500 | 0.000000 | 0.002651 | 0.000000 |
| pronouns_he_vs_she | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 |

## Did ranking quality change?
| metric | task11_as_shipped | task11_text_only | task12_fair | difference_fair_minus_as_shipped | difference_fair_minus_text_only |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Precision@5 | 0.920000 | 0.920000 | 0.920000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 |
| Recall@5 | 0.538014 | 0.538014 | 0.538014 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 |
| NDCG@5 | 0.911531 | 0.922600 | 0.921251 | 0.009720 | -0.001348 |
| Top-5 Hits | 46.000000 | 46.000000 | 46.000000 | 0.000000 | 0.000000 |

Same Task 11 labels and methodology (10 jobs, 555 labeled resume-job rows; labels used only for evaluation). Versus shipped Task 11: Precision@5, Recall@5, Top-5 Hits unchanged; NDCG@5 changed by +0.0097 and the top-5 sets differ in 3 of 10 jobs. The fair screener keeps degree text (which Task 11 scrubbed) and masks only the institution tier, so a small ranking change is expected and is not caused by protected attributes. Versus the text-only run the NDCG@5 difference is -0.0013 (its top-5 sets differ from shipped in 3 jobs). With 10 jobs and 95 relevant candidates, differences of this size are within noise: they show that the fairness change did not meaningfully reduce ranking quality, and they must not be read as an accuracy gain.

## Limitations
* Only 25 twins are available; the paired changes primarily test gender-coded names and sometimes college tier. No conclusions are made for unrepresented protected groups or intersections.
* The supplied twins cannot test every personal-information pathway. Synthetic perturbations are not evidence about real applicants. Real resumes contain many more potential proxies (hobbies, employers, schools by name, gaps, locations).
* Equal scores for twins do not show the screener is fair: group-level gaps were observed (`group_gap_report.csv`, fair screener, all_resumes (185)): gender 0.0138 (group means {"Female": 0.379227, "Male": 0.365467}); tier 0.0344 (group means {"Tier 1": 0.384752, "Tier 2": 0.350384, "Tier 3": 0.383071}). These aggregates do not establish treatment effects; monitor them with appropriate job-related and legal context.
* Job-stratified audit (`job_stratified_group_gap.csv`; only groups with at least 3 resumes enter a job-level gap): gender: mean job-level max gap 0.0413 across 10 jobs; largest 0.0689 in J02; candidate-weighted job-centered score means (Female +0.0114, Male -0.0076); tier: mean job-level max gap 0.1099 across 9 jobs; largest 0.2055 in J08; candidate-weighted job-centered score means (Tier 1 +0.0116, Tier 2 -0.0190, Tier 3 +0.0120). Group score differences co-move with required-skill overlap and human suitability in this small sample; labels may be biased. No protected-group score adjustment was applied because it would change candidate treatment using the protected attribute without evidence that these differences are unfair model errors. Keep protected attributes audit-only and review job-specific outcomes and labels before any policy change.
* Human labels, used to evaluate quality, may themselves be biased. The names are Indian-context fictional names; results may not transfer.
* Name masking uses a header heuristic; unusual layouts, multi-line names or names in free text could be missed. Re-audit on new data.

## Who decides the accuracy-fairness trade-off?
*"If fixing the fairness gap lowers accuracy a little, who decides what trade-off is acceptable?"* Not the model builder alone, and not accuracy by default.
Fairness and accuracy should not be treated as competing goals in which accuracy automatically wins. The acceptable trade-off should be decided through **transparent governance** that includes
affected stakeholders (candidates and their representatives), HR professionals, legal / compliance teams and responsible-AI experts. A small reduction in ranking performance may be acceptable if it meaningfully reduces
discriminatory outcomes; the decision must be supported by evidence (like the tables above), documented, reviewed and monitored over time. In this audit the largest observed ranking-quality drop was -0.0013; whether that is acceptable is exactly the governance decision described above.

**Equal accuracy does not mean equal treatment.** Two systems can have identical Precision@5 or NDCG@5 while treating similar candidates differently - for example, a screener that ranks twin resumes differently can still
have the same average accuracy, because errors for one group can offset errors for another. Accuracy is an average over a population; equal treatment is a property of how comparable individuals are scored,
which is why counterfactual twins and group audits are needed in addition to accuracy metrics. The ranking is a decision-support tool, not an automatic hiring decision.
